idiom_name: fixed-width message header struct + static dispatch table
implementation_notes: C has no metadata channel of its own, so the property section is whatever the protocol or your own framing defines: a small header with a type field (netlink's struct nlmsghdr, whose nlmsg_type is documented as "Type of message content", is the canonical in-kernel example) or a magic/length/type triple in front of the body. Nothing in the standard library replaces the classic structure - you hand-write a static table of token-to-parse-function pairs and dispatch on the type field before the body is touched. A fixed-size integer or enum token beats a string token because dispatch stays a bounds-checked table index instead of a parse.
pitfalls: Casting the raw buffer to a struct assumes alignment and no padding; use a byte-wise accessor or an explicitly packed header, otherwise the type field itself is garbage on some ABIs.
Read and validate the length before trusting the type field: a header parsed past the end of the buffer is a classic out-of-bounds read.
An unknown type must be rejected, not skipped - silently ignoring it turns a protocol error into a hang or a mis-parse.
